ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: the road league, the hospitallers and the herders
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Rimfolk adds three peoples of peaceful callings to the world: a road league of caravan masters and waystation keepers, an order of hospitallers who keep sickhouses, and nomad herders who follow the grass with great herds. Each has its own gear, colours, faith, towns and words, and turns up in Rimfolk's camps, asks, callers and letters in its own way.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: They are among the world's peoples when a new world is made, once each, at the game's usual chances; remove them in the world's faction list like any other people. A save made before they were there meets them when one of them arises during play (the page on new peoples that arise). Four more came later: the pilgrims, the scholars, the spacer enclave and the river folk have a page of their own.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: All three are mostly peaceful. They defend their towns, and they raid only when the colony has turned them hostile, by the game's own rules, and less often than other peoples then. Their notables have titles of their own, their messengers words of their own, and their towns a plan of their own when the land suits it.

li.heading: Who they are

table.li: People | Lives by | Age | On the map | Their towns
The road league | Trade on the roads | Industrial | Coats dyed teal of every cut; guards in one kit of duster, hat and flak | Few: walled waystations where roads meet
The hospitaller order | Healing | Medieval | An ivory habit of any cut; sworn guards in ivory plate, lay archers | Sickhouses round an herb garden
The herding folk | Their herds | Tribal | Hides of every make, russet caps and coats; wardens in war veils | Camps of round houses and pens

li.after: With Ideology each keeps a faith of its own (a creed of the road, the open hand, the long grass) and its own style; with Biotech each has a share of other kinds of people (hussars and genies with the league, yttakin and pigskins with the herders). With Vanilla Ideology Expanded's memes their faiths take a meme of trade and of the waymasters leading together, of healthcare and of the lamp's light, or of nomads and of their elders too.

li.heading: Where their ways began
li.text: Each keeps a founding story, a few sayings, and what it honours and fears. Their card shows what they honour and fear and one of their sayings, and their letters, messengers, visitors and talk speak from them. A people that arises in their ways keeps those ways too.

points.li: The road league began at Harrow Ford, where the road belonged to whoever had the most rifles, until a carter named Edda Vane asked every waymaster on the road for one guard and one wagon and took them through the ford under nine flags. The league keeps the Waystone Book: fair dealers in good ink, robbers in red. They say "every crate home" and "a word given at the waystone stands"; they honour the kept word and a fair price, and fear the robber and a road nobody keeps.

The hospitaller order began with Aldith, a carter's daughter who nursed a fever town alone through a winter and in the spring hung its last lamp over the sickhouse door for anyone who came, raiders included. Every sickhouse keeps a lamp lit and the Book of the Spared. They say "we were spared, and so we owe" and "nobody on a sickbed is anyone's enemy"; they honour the spared and the night watch, and fear the fever's return and a door shut on the sick.

The herding folk began in the year the wells failed, when a herd girl named Tamsa walked the last forty head through the dust to grass nobody believed in and brought every one home. Herders still count every beast at dusk because she did. They say "the grass will tell" and "never leave a beast on the road"; they honour a guest at the fire and good grass, and fear the dry year, the thief and a fence across the drove roads.

li.heading: What they wear, carry and know
li.text: No two of them look alike, but each people is known by its colour on a piece or two. Their soldiers wear one kit, their civilians whatever their age and calling would, drawn from the game, the DLCs and the mods loaded (the Vanilla Expanded apparel, armour, accessories and weapons sets, Vanilla Factions Expanded's medieval, tribal, classical and settlers' gear, Vanilla Ideology Expanded's hats, Rimsenal's and Advanced Armaments' guns, Melee Animation's lassos). With no mods at all the base game's gear dresses and arms every one of them. Pawns already in a game keep what they have; new ones come dressed this way.

points.li: The road league: wayfarers and factors in a teal coat of any cut over travelling clothes, now and then a fez, a pack or a tool belt, with frontier revolvers and rifles where Vanilla Weapons Expanded's Frontier set is loaded; caravan guards and outriders in the league's kit of teal duster, cowboy hat and flak with an ammo pack, the outriders with a lasso; the master in fine clothes and a top hat. Wayfarers carry beer, cloth, wine or a little silver, now and then a map. A few wayfarers are wayfarers or bards of A RimWorld of Magic, a few of the guards and outriders sharpshooters or gladiators, and now and then the league master is a commander.

The hospitaller order: the habit is shared but not its cut or its age, an ivory robe or mantle worn thin or new, with a hood, a cap, a skullcap, a headscarf or now and then a plague doctor's mask, and prayer beads, now and then a prior in a bishop's mitre; the sworn guards in matching ivory plate and helmet, with Medieval 2 the order's ivory tabard and a heater shield; the lay archers in an ivory cape and helmet with a quiver, bows or arbalests. Hospitallers carry herbs and clean cloth, salves and candles, a medicinal quill. Some of the hospitallers and their prior are priests of A RimWorld of Magic, a few of the sworn guards paladins and of the lay archers rangers.

The herding folk: hides and wraps of every make, russet on their tail caps, wraps and coats, a lasso at the hip for the beasts; their herd wardens in war veils and war wraps; archers with quivers and javelins, herders with slings. Herders carry hay, hides, wool or butter. Their elder is often a druid, a few archers are rangers and a few wardens gladiators.

Their kinds of people (Biotech) are a real mix, and still mostly baseliners: genies, highmates, lowmates, drakonori, high elves and orangutans among the hospitallers; yttakin, neanderthals, animusen, boarskins, venators, saurids, wood elves and gorillas with the herders; hussars, genies, boglegs, stoneborn, uhlans, starjacks, bonobos and a few androids on the league's roads, each where its mod is loaded.

The road league: when the game sends a trader caravan, the league's is three times as likely as another people's, with rich and varied stock and plenty of guards. Its market folk, salt caravans, far merchants and road wardens camp on the colony's land more often. An outrider may come ahead of a caravan to ask whether it should turn aside to the colony, and the league may ask the colony's caravan to walk one of its factors home with the season's silver. When the snow closes the roads in winter, a league caravan may ask for winter quarters by the colony: a long camp that trades all the while, its road wardens ready to stand with the colony if raiders come, and the Waystone Book to be written in; after a stay that went well, its caravan master leaves a carved waystone in its crate at the colony's gate as they go. A neighbour's patrol after robbers likeliest is the league's.

The hospitaller order: its healers, herb-gatherers, pilgrims and penitents camp more often. One of its hospitallers may stop at the gate for a colonist with an everyday ailment and see to it for nothing; the colony may send medicine back for the sickhouse. In a plague year the order asks the colony for medicine by a set day, and a call for a healer to help at a sickhouse comes from the order likeliest. Travellers who lodge at one of its sickhouses come home tended, as if they had carried medicine. When one of the colony is down with a fever (an illness the body has to fight off: flu, plague, malaria, an infection), a hospitaller may come to go from bed to bed, four at most and the sickest first, with care that helps the body fight it off for a day and a half, and stay the night; the colony's doctor may work alongside and learn, and medicine go back to the sickhouse. A herb-gatherer at the gate likeliest is the order's.

The herding folk: their caravans walk a herd of eight to fourteen beasts for sale beside their pack animals, and come half again as often. Their drovers, shearers and beast-catchers camp more often, and in the fall and the winter they ask to graze a herd of up to a dozen head on the colony's land for the cold months. The drove roads and the great herds come for them likeliest, and the ask for fodder for a herd; a herder at the gate with a thirsty or sick herd, or drovers on the way to a fair, likeliest are theirs. After a winter's grazing that went well, the camp elder hands over a young beast of the herd at the colony's gate as they go, the colony's from then on.
Their towns' heads are waymasters, priors and prioresses, and camp elders; their traders are caravan masters, cellarers and drovers; their messengers are road riders, postulants and riders.
Their letters, their messengers at the gate and the talk with them are in their own voice, as each people's age is in its own.

A town of theirs, when its map is made, is laid out to their plan: the league's walled yard with stalls and a storehouse, the order's long ward of sixteen beds and its cloister, the herders' round houses and two great pens with their herd in them. Where the land is too wet or rough for it, the game makes its own base.

li.heading: Their age over the years
li.text: All of Rimfolk's peoples, these three and the twelve others, and every people that arises in their ways, move between the ages as the years pass. Each is looked at once a season. It comes toward the next age at a pace of its own ways, faster for what the colony does with it, and falls back an age when it is cut off from the world. A letter in their own voice tells each change, and their card and the region's page of peoples say which age they live in and which way they are heading, and why.

points.li: Their own pace: the learned society, the Stormglass Conclave and the road league soonest, the Kiln Guild soon for a medieval people, the herders and the Mossborn latest. Each takes no more than its ways would: the hospitallers stop at the industrial age by their faith, as do the wardens, the river folk, the pilgrims and the Quiet Bell, the herders too, and the Mossborn at the medieval age. The spacer enclave is at the height of what anyone knows already.

What quickens them: trade with the colony over the year (twice the pace at 5000 silver), gifts of books, techprints, components or tools (in a caravan's gift, the trade window's gift or a pod), their young who learn at the colony (the Conclave's apprentice of the sky, the guild's journeyman on the wander-year, a ward fostered) and their masters who teach the colony's people, and an alliance or a pact. Three times their own pace at most.

What sets them back: nobody's trade for years, their towns burned in fights, and war with most of the world. One of these alone sets no people back; more of them together do, an age in five to ten years, and never more than an age below the one they began in.
In a typical game of five to ten years a few peoples reach the next age, and a learned one the colony helps a great deal may go two.

What changes with a people's age: its next visitors, traders and fighters come dressed and armed as the new age is (bows and swords for a league fallen back to the medieval age, guns for the herders in the industrial age, and nothing of a later age among a people that fell back), its camps are built the new age's way, its traders carry the new age's goods, and its words, messengers and letters take the new age's form. People of theirs already in the world keep what they have.
Setting: "Peoples' ages change", on by default. Off, every people lives in the age it began in.
